maintopic: DEATH OF MR. THOMAS HERBERT LENNOX TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY BY MR. GUTHRIE, MR. MACKENZIE KING, MR. COOTE AND MR. POULIOT

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. THOMAS HERBERT LENNOX TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY BY MR. GUTHRIE, MR. MACKENZIE KING, MR. COOTE AND MR. POULIOT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it becomes my painful duty in the absence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to announce in this chamber the sudden death of our esteemed colleague, Thomas Herbert Lennox which, I believe, occurred in the city of Toronto at an early hour this morning. The awful suddenness of the demise of our late colleague has cast a feeling of most profound sorrow throughout this chamber. It was but a few days ago that he sat in his place here and also but a few days ago when he was engaged in an important legal case before the Supreme Court of Canada. Little did we think at that time that he was so soon to be removed from this earthly scene. It brings before us very prominently the old admonition that in the midst of life we are in death.
Mr. Lennox had sat in this parliament for a number of years and I think I can say he had endeared himself to members in every corner of the house. His affable, genial disposition was manifest at all times and his friends throughout Ontario and in this chamber were legion. He was a native son of the province of Ontario, having been born sixty-five years ago in the county of Simcoe. He was the product of the public schools of Ontario and of the collegiate institute at Barrie. Afterwards he took his legal course and was called to the bar at Osgoode Hall in the city of Toronto. After having been called to the bar he immediately engaged in practice and from the very start of his career at the bar it may be said that he was wonderfully successful. He soon rose to a very prominent position at the bar; he was made one of His Majesty's counsel
Death of Mr. Lennox

learned in the law; he was elected a bencher of the Law Society of Upper Canada, and at the time of his death he was one of the undoubted leaders of the bar of the province of Ontario and one of the really great lawyers of the Dominion of Canada. His death will be sincerely mourned by his many colleagues in the legal profession. The late T. H. Lennox was a man of varied attainment and of many activities. During the war it will be remembered that he was exceedingly active; at that time, he cast aside his profession and his public life, and through his efforts to a very large extent the battalion known as the 208th was raised, he himself became the officer commanding, with the rank of lieutenant-colonel, and took that battalion overseas. He returned to Canada with an excellent military record.
Early in life our late colleague resolved to devote at least some portion of his time to what we might term the public service of the country, though I think it will be recognized on all sides that his chief interest in secular matters was in his own chosen profession of law. He devoted a very large amount of his time to his profession, he was engaged in a great many varied and important cases, and was not permitted to devote as much time to his public life as we would all have liked. As early as the year 1902 he unsuccessfully contested a riding for the legislature of the province of Ontario, but subsequently in the jrear 1905 he was elected for the provincial constituency of North York at a general election, and at four subsequent general elections in the province of Ontario he carried the same riding. He continued as a member of the Ontario legislature until he was first returned to the House of Commons as representative for the riding of North York in the general election of 1925, again in the year 1926 he was elected for that riding, and also in the year 1930 at the last general election.
He has had an eminently successful career both in the legislature of Ontario and in the parliament of Canada, and had he been able to devote more time to his parliamentary duties he would certainly have risen to a very high place in the public life of Canada. He was a man whom everyone liked, everyone regarded as a friend. While he was a hard fighter when a contest was on, he was a man who carried no bitterness, no acrimonious feelings when the contest was over. I believe one can say that all who knew him were his friends; few, if any, were his enemies. The suddenness of his taking off has produced a tremendous impression in this house. We all mourn him most sincerely. All we can do now is to lament his loss and express our

feelings of regret and sympathy to those members of his family and relatives who survive.
It is to be noted that the deceased himself received some hard knocks during his lifetime. Only a few months ago his only son was suddenly killed in an automobile accident in the city of Toronto. Indeed, many of his intimate friends consider that Thomas Herbert Lennox never really got over the shock caused by his son's death.
He is gone from us, and all we can do is to respect his memory and lament his early death.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. THOMAS HERBERT LENNOX TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY BY MR. GUTHRIE, MR. MACKENZIE KING, MR. COOTE AND MR. POULIOT
speechtext:
On behalf of
honourable members of the official opposition, I desire to convey to the Prime Minister, to members of the government, and to other honourable gentlemen opposite the expression of our sympathy in the loss which they have sustained in the death of one of their fellow members of this House of Commons, one who for many years had been prominent as a member of the Conservative party in the province of Ontario.
In the appreciation which he has just expressed of the late member's career, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has reviewed in a fitting manner Mr. Lennox's attainments and services, alike to his profession and to the state. I join with him in recognition of the late member's talents and abilities,' and in particular of his patriotic services at the time of the great war, to which the minister has made special reference.
As one who, for a short time, had the honour of representing the constituency of North York, I have knowledge of the considerable personal and political following which the late member enjoyed in that riding, and I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to express to Mr. Lennox's friends in the constituency my sympathy with them in the death of one to whom, over a period of so many years, they have given so large a measure of their confidence and support.
I also join, as all on this side will wish very sincerely to join, in the expression of sympathy for Mrs. Lennox who has been so suddenly and so greatly bereaved.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. THOMAS HERBERT LENNOX TRIBUTES TO HIS MEMORY BY MR. GUTHRIE, MR. MACKENZIE KING, MR. COOTE AND MR. POULIOT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) is not here. In his absence I would like to take the opportunity of saying that I am sure every member in this corner of the house joins very heartily in the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and the leader of the opposi-

Oaths oj Allegiance Act
tion (Mr. Mackenzie King) expressing our regret at the death of Colonel Lennox and our sympathy with his relatives and friends. May I say that I doubt if there is a member of the House of Commons who was more generally liked by his fellow members than was Colonel Lennox. I think that is one of the highest tributes that can be paid to any member.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS PO'ULIOT (Tem-iscouata): Mr. Speaker, when I declared my pair yesterday with the hon. member for North York nothing was further from my mind than that the flag would fly at half mast over this building to-day as a tribute to his memory. For nearly ten years or sessions he was my pair, and I shall always have the most pleasant recollections of my dealings with the late hon. gentleman. We have been closely associated and I came to have the highest respect for his qualities. He had attained prominence at the bar of his province and at the bar of this country; he was a gallant soldier, he was a congenial member of this house, a very popular representative of the people, and1 a true friend. I join in the tributes which have been expressed to his memory, and wish to convey my most heartfelt and sincere sympathy to his family, to the members of the legal profession in the province of Ontario and in Canada at large, and also to my hon. friends .on the other side of the house.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 57, to amend the Oaths of Allegiance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill really takes the place of a bill that was introduced by the former Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). After the hon. gentleman introduced his bill on March 13 last I conferred with him at the earliest opportunity, and it seemed expedient to suggest to him that the bill might take a slightly different form. After consultation with the hon. gentleman he withdrew his bill, with the result that the present bill was introduced on April 19 and fully explained to the house. In effect it is carrying out a resolution of the imperial conference of 1926 at which Canada was represented by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his colleague the then Minister of Justice. That resolution of the imperial conference was carried into effect by the parliament of the United Kingdom, which passed the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act, 1927, and on May 13, 1927, a royal proclamation was issued setting out His Majesty's style and title.
The oath of allegiance, as it appears in the present bill, is identical with the oath of allegiance as administered in Great Britain, in Australia, in the Union of South Africa and I think generally throughout the British Empire ; and it is deemed expedient that the same oath of allegiance should be prescribed in Canada. I think, as far as hon. members have expressed opinions to me privately, this bill meets with the almost unanimous support of the house, and as I fully explained it on the previous occasion it seems to me that no further explanation is required at the present time.

speechtext: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved the second reading of Bill No. 70, to amend the Food and Drugs Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It is entirely at the option of the house as to whether or not

any discussion takes place at the present time. Perhaps I might explain the bill a little further than I did on the motion for first reading. The main objects of the amendments in the amending bill are to produce a conformity between the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act and the Food and Drugs Act. Under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act there is a provision whereby in the case of certain diseases it is not permissible to sell certain drugs or remedies. That provision does not obtain in the Food and Drugs Act. It so happens that when on some occasions people find it is not permissible to sell remedies under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act they seek permission for the sale of such remedies under the Food and Drugs Act. As the object of the provision under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act with reference to the prevention of the sale of certain remedies for the treatment of certain diseases is for the protection of the public, and as time may be lost in the event of people acting on advertisements of those remedies, these changes are proposed to the Food and Drugs Act.
Another provision presents the adulteration of vinegar through the use of acetic acid. Then, there is a schedule of diseases for which remedies may not be sold. There is provision whereby in the light of subsequent knowledge, changes in the list of diseases and list of remedies may be made by order in council. From time to time therefore, if found desirable, certain changes may be effected by order in council.

With the principle of the bill I have much sympathy, because I understand that it is directed against sales by people commonly known as quacks, and with a view to protection against such people. Although I have much sympathy with the measure there are some features in it with which I cannot agree in toto. For instance, as I understand the bill, any remedies which may be self-administered can no longer be imported, manufactured or offered for sale. I have in mind this case: I understand that for the treatment of arteriosclerosis there are certain standard drugs prescribed by the medical profession, but which the profession do not compound. One goes to his medical adviser who prescribes a certain medicine or solvent. These medicines are already made up; the patient goes to the drug store and presents the medical prescription. The druggist takes pills from a bottle and puts them into a box, and after the box is labelled we are allowed to take it home. From the drug store we may purchase some medicine which has been imported or manufactured. If the bill now before us became law I understand that I could not go to a drug store to buy some of these specific remedies declared to be valuable in the softening of arteries, or when used as a solvent.
Let us suppose that we are suffering from blood poisoning. What would be my position if, going to camp, I decided to take iodine, mercurochrome, listerine, peroxide, or some other medicines which could be used in the event of an accident? In a case of blood poisoning those remedies would be self-administered. We know that blood poisoning may be caused from an interior condition, or from a scratch. Supposing I happened to be in the woods, and while walking I tripped, thereby causing some part of my body to become infected, under this measure I could not have iodine or mercurochrome. I could not take one of those disinfectants to my camp, nor could I import, manufacture, offer for sale or advertise by any means whatever, nor sell any remedy 74726-1751
recommended or suggested for use for selfadministration. That would be my difficulty. I suppose if this bill passed the country storekeeper would not be at leisure to sell any more painkiller, because it might be used to combat blood poisoning, or some such ailment. To what extent should we be limited because it was a self-administered drug? For instance, when I go to camp I might want to take with me spirits of ammonia. It might be for a case of chronic heart disease or for a heart attack that might suddenly develop. As I interpret this clause I could not take up with me spirits of ammonia because it was going to be self-administered. Clause 2 reads:
No person shall import, manufacture, offer for saleany of these drugs that might be self-administered.
It is quite true that pills have been sold for a large number of diseases, and I fully agree that the public should be protected; but take obesity, for example. There is the glandular kind, and obesity that results from over-eating and under-exercising. As I understand the effect of this bill the remedy for obesity of the glandular kind would be barred. That might be all right. But to what extent would this prohibition apply to treatment by way of dieting, plus the use of some drug, probably laxatives, which are sometimes used. I have a lot of sympathy with the principle of the bill but I would suggest that it be referred to a mixed committee of medical men, who I suppose are the ones primarily interested, and practical men-I am not saying that offensively-so that the Food and Drugs Act might be considered both from the point of view of the medical men and of protecting the rights and privileges of the public. We do not want the ordinary rights of the people trampled upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I do not think that the interpretation placed upon this amendment by my hon. friend from Ottawa is a correct one. The amendment does not propose to prohibit the manufacture of any remedy. It proposes to prohibit the sale or manufacture of any remedy for self-administration in the case of the diseases which are listed under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act and which it is thought can be placed, with advantage to the public, under the Food and Drugs Act. That is a different thing altogether. It altogether depends on the objective. This amendment does not prohibit the manufacture of the remedy but it says that the remedy must not be manufactured or sold or advertised for certain diseases or conditions, which is a different thing altogether.
Food and Drugs Act

lam not satisfied with the explanation that has just been given by the minister. I have the greatest respect and the kindliest feelings for him, and he knows it, and I do not intend to quarrel with him at all. I stated at the outset that I agreed with the principle of the bill to protect people from themselves. But I ask the minister, will this bill prevent me taking iodine, for instance, to my camp? The bill says that you cannot sell or manufacture these remedies which are to be self-administered. Of course, if a doctor prescribes the use of that remedy it would be all right, but I am speaking of iodine that is going to be self-administered, and which, as I read clause 2, cannot be imported, manufactured or offered for sale. I should like the minister to make sub-clause 6A plain. I cannot get it. Under its provisions you cannot even offer for sale or advertise any of these antiseptics that may be used in the case of blood-poisoning. Of course, I agree that one would have to determine what bloodpoisoning was. But suppose it was caused by a scratch; how, under this clause, am I going to use iodine or listerine or lysol or any of these other antiseptics. I am not here to advertise these products by mentioning their names. Take any antiseptic that might be used for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
What the amendment
seeks to correct is self-administration in the case of diseases where valuable time may be lost and recovery delayed by self-administration instead of medical treatment. I do not think it is a reasonable interpretation to say that one could not under this clause make an application of iodine to the skin. It is the advertising of remedies for self-administration in the treatment of these diseases and their sale to the public for that purpose that we are seeking to prevent. The public at the present time very often depend on these advertisements and believe that they are going to obtain benefit from these remedies, when such is not the case.

I would ask the
minister if the object of this legislation is to restrict the sale of proprietary articles, commonly called patent medicines, by druggists.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
This amendment does
not affect what my hon. friend refers to in the slightest.
I am only asking if it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
And I am simply
answering my hon. friend's question. This has nothing to do with patent medicines.

They come under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act. This is the Food and Drugs Act, and this amendment does not touch the sale or prohibition of sale of patent medicines. It is limiting the sale of certain remedies for the treatment of certain diseases under the Food and Drugs Act. The question of patent medicines does not come directly under the amendment.

I presume, Mr. Chairman, that we are discussing clause 6A of section 2. I did not know that we had dealt with section 1. But if we are discussing clause 6A I take it to mean, and I would ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong, that remedies such as might be prescribed for diseases listed in schedule A shall not be imported, manufactured, advertised or offered for sale by others than qualified medical men. I assume that is the meaning of the clause. If the clause is so sweeping as to mean that no pharmaceutical company, medical man or anyone else shall import a remedy which may be prescribed for the treatment of arteriosclerosis, let us say, or Bright's disease, in my opinion it is too broad. If, on the other hand, the bill is intended to prohibit other than medical men or qualified persons from importing and offering for sale medicines of a nature not safe for one not posted to take without directions, then I think the clause is entirely in order. I should like an explanation from the minister in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The amendment states
that it shall not be for selfadministration.
Once a remedy is recommended by the label on the bottle it becomes a remedy recommended and you cannot sell it.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Recommended
for self-administration only.

You may have a painkiller which could be self-administered in the bush to prevent a cold. The label might state that it is a preventative of colds, but you would not be able to sell it, to advertise it, to manufacture it or to import it because it is recommended and is to be self-administered.

Get the other
fellow to give you a dose and then it would not be self-administered.

My hon. friends may
know what it means but I do not. I am in favour of the spirit of the bill but I think we should be able to understand it.

If the hon. member will
read section 6A a little more carefully he

Food and Drugs Act
will see that it has nothing at all to do with common colds. It refers to the diseases mentioned in schedule A which are of such a nature that remedies prescribed or self-administered without the supervision of someone who understands the disease might be harmful to the individual and may even endanger or imperil his life if there was any delay. I think all medical members of the house will agree that remedies for the diseases mentioned in this schedule should be carefully prescribed and taken only on the instructions of a qualified medical practitioner.

Suppose a man has blood poisoning and he purchases one of these disinfectants which are recommended for the cure of blood poisoning, perhaps by superficial application. These remedies are recommended and suggested for that purpose and I want to know how they would be affected by this bill. I did not draft the bill and I am trying to get an interpretation of its meaning. This is the time to get that interpretation, not when we get into court. I ask the minister or someone in authority if, after this bill goes through, I will be able to purchase one of these disinfectants which are recommended or suggested for blood poisoning and which may be self-administered.

I think that difficulty could be overcome by adding just a word or two to the clause. The hon. member is confusing external applications with internal medication. It looks to me as though the schedule contains one or two diseases which could be left out, I think influenza and probably alcoholism could be left out. The rest of the diseases are of such a sierious nature that a medical man ought to be called in immediately. There are no known medicinal cures for some of the diseases mentioned, surgery is the only method by which a cure can be effected. The hon. member is referring to remedies such as lysol which are not taken internally. I do not think there is anything in this bill to prevent a man from using that remedy externally. If there is, I suggest that the words "for internal medication" be added. We must protect the public against themselves and against their own foolishness. We must protect them against deception. This is in the interests of their health and even of their lives. For instance, take cancer. Everyone knows that it runs a certain length of time before it breaks away from its original moorings or location. If that happens the patient is doomed. Time is important in this disease, as it is in tetanus, or what is commonly known as lockjaw. In nearly all
these cases time is an essential factor and drugs are mostly useless. I think I would be safe in saying that there is not a disease in this category in which medicine would be worth anything as far as effecting a cure is concerned. There is great danger in the delay which may occur by the application of these quack remedies, and the patient may lose his life.
Mr. EiLLIOTT: I think the discussion could be clarified a good deal if the minister would tell us what is meant by "recommended or suggested for use." Influenza is one of the diseases mentioned in schedule A and of those mentioned it is perhaps the one most frequently treated by home remedies or by remedies obtained from the drug store. After this bill becomes law, could a person having influenza go to the drug store and purchase a remedy which states on its label that it is good for influenza? Will that be permitted, or will he have no right to do that? I do not think he should have a right to go to a druggist and say, "I have influenza, what do you recommend for it?" I take it that the druggist must not suggest that a particular remedy is good for influenza. As I understand the meaning of this bill, after it becomes law no one will be able to go to a drug store and purchase a remedy for any of these diseases when the label on the bottle or the verbal representation of the druggist is to the effect that it is recommended as being good for any one of these diseases.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I think the interprets tion given by my hon. friend is approximately correct; it is nearer the truth than that given by other hon. gentlemen. We have heard the old time honoured remedy referred to more than once to-day, and that is painkiller, but painkiller does not come under this amendment or under this act. There is some confusion on the part of some hon. gentlemen about this matter. Painkiller finds its resting place, I believe, under the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act and it is dealt with there; whether it may or may not be sold is determined under that act; it does not come under our proposed amendment.
With reference to influenza, that is no light matter. Does my hon. friend realize the last year in Canada, for which a report is available, there were 4,500 deaths from that disease, so it is a highly important subject. Let us take afflictions that are familiar to us, for instance, the case of lockjaw, which is another name for tetanus; if the sufferer, on the advice of some kind friend, resorts to some remedy that the latter has found good, it may be for
Food and Drugs Act

something else, the time has gone by for the remedy that we know is practically the only one that is helpful and curative in tetanus or lockjaw, and that is by administering antitoxin.
These are striking examples and as we know we may come down to a boundary line; that is natural in all matters of legislation. As we are all aware it is of the first importance to act at once in the case of diphtheria, and how? By administering an antitoxin. Some friend or next door neighbour can hardly be a safe adviser in such cases. The whole measure is one designed to protect the public. One constantly hears about cancer to which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has referred. What do we all hear? If this had been dealt with earlier, the prospects of success would have been substantially good. In cancer there are probably .two remedies that are of use: one is by surgical operation, removing, if possible, the cancer, and the other is by administering radium or X-ray. There are no successful remedies other than those I have mentioned, and if a neighbour or somebody else suggests some remedy, the opportunity for the man or woman who is trying to treat it in this way, is slipping fast, That is all.

I have no doubt that the aim of the bill is to protect the public from the misuse or abuse of medicines, but I think the whole trouble is that the wording of the bill is not very clear. The real trouble is about the word "remedy." Drugs are either crude or compound and crude may be open to the public as to its name and purpose while compound may also be open to the public with the prescription written on the bottle, or it may be patented with a secret prescription. The clause reads:
Nor sell any remedy-
What kind of remedy? Is it crude, open prescription or patent medicine? If the wording comprises patent medicine, it should read:
Nor sell any remedy recommended or suggested and labelled for use for selfadministration.
I know for a fact that in the patent medicine branch there is a board of supervisors of patent medicines or patent prescriptions coming in and anything that is harmful is not accepted. This bill is to prohibit the importation, manufacture, offering for sale, advertising by any means whatever or selling of any remedy recommended or suggested in the case of certain diseases. It is to forbid a person or a company to put on the market a medicine recommended by advertisement or by pamphlet or in any other way such as by the label on the bottle, that it is to cure some of the diseases mentioned. Those diseases are
fMr. MacLaren.]
considered by the supervisors of medicine serious enough that they should not be meddled with by anybody except those qualified. Therefore I think the clause should read:
Any remedy recommended or labelled for use for self-administration in the treatment of any of the diseases-
And so forth. I think that would cover the whole point.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find that what he is suggesting now is already covered in the act. All of those remedies that come under the Food and Drugs Act have the formula on the bottle or the case or whatever it may be. Let us say the bottle; the formula now has to appear on it That I understand is what my hon. friend has been suggesting and that now is operative under the act.
Under which act? The Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act?

I would like to ask the minister one last question. He has spoken about influenza. There is influenza and influenza. We know at one time an influenza epidemic caused us a great deal of harm, trouble and death. But we are in the habit of calling grippe and cold by the same name. My question is this: If I call that cold or grippe, influenza; if I go to a corner drugstore and buy quinine which is recommended and suggested by everybody and this is contained in a box labelled "quinine, infallibly recommended for influenza, grippe and colds," what happens to me and what will be the position of the man who sells it?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
speaking outside the provisions of the act. I will say first that this has nothing to do with proprietary or patent medicines. They are dealt with in another act. The hon. gentleman mentions certain articles and asks whether under the conditions indicated they could or could not be sold. Now let us get down to what we really have before us. This amendment deals with such remedies as are not permitted to be sold under this act for certain purposes, and the question as to quinine does not arise, because as I say these remedies must have the formulae on the bottles.

Where do we get that? It is not in the bill.

Food and Drugs Act

speechtext: We find it in the Food and Drugs Act, chapter 76, revised statutes of Canada, 1927.

That would be a

I think there is no

Before going further I think I ought to call the attention of the committee to the fact that we are discussing section 2, whereas section 1 has not yet been dealt with.

I put a question to
the minister. He told me the bill does not
restrict the sale of certain articles although he told the hon. member for West Middlesex that it does. Was his answer to me correct or incorrect?

I am listening very patiently.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: But not clearly. I think that is a correct choice of words. I do not conceal this fact, that it is difficult to frame that provision so clearly that those listening perhaps for the first time follow it exactly. It does not contemplate the suppression of the manufacture of drugs of all kinds nor does it say that a remedy like, say, quinine cannot be sold. Those are the very ones that are affected. That is what I am trying to make clear. Now it may be that that clause is not as clear as it might be. That would be under subsection 6A and I presume section 1, that has not been discussed at all. I would like to say a word about that. Should there be at any time reason to change that list of diseases or should there be reason for change in certain remedies mentioned in schedule B, it should be provided that those changes could be effected by order in council. Otherwise it would mean coming back to the house for an amendment. Science advances from year to year, knowledge increases continuously. Indians: to provide for expenses connected with the administration of Indian Affairs, including salaries, supplies, relief, medical attendance, hospitalization, dwellings, agricultural activities, surveys, roads, bridges, irrigation, dyking, education, etc., and a grant of $100,000 approved by parliament in session of 1926-27, $3,939,500.
Would the minister tell the committee what agricultural activities are carried on under this vote?

In the different provinces, notably in Ontario and the western provinces, and to a lesser degree in British Columbia, Quebec and the maritimes, Indians carry on agricultural pursuits on reserves which are suitable for such a vocation. In Ontario there are certain reserves, such as the Six Nations reserve at Brantford, and the Tyendinaga reserve along the Bay of Quinte, as well as others throughout the province, where the Indians carry on farming operations in the same manner as they are carried on by their white neighbours, and the same condition applies in the west, where there are many reserves large in area and located in fertile regions.
Mr. MoINTOSH: Will the minister explain what advance the Indians are making in the way of agricultural development?

In connection with the residential schools farms are operated, and the children are given instruction not only in reading, writing, arithmetic and the usual courses of study prescribed for public school but also practical instruction by the heads of the institutions in the different phases of agriculture, such as the care of cattle, swine and horses and the growing of crops. This practice has been in effect for a great many years, and I am happy to tell the committee that we in the department believe progress is being made to quite an extent. As the committee knows, in the past the Indians were not an agricultural people; they were rather a pastoral people or, shall we say, devoted to

the chase. During the years that this policy has been in effect, however, the children of the second generation have made appreciable progress. Those who first attended these schools may not have made that progress which we could have wished, but we have found that it is the custom of the pupils of those various residential schools to intermarry, and on going to the schools their children are noticeably more intelligent and more interested in agriculture.

I have two Indian reserves in my constituency, Maria and Restigouche. A few days ago I sent the minister a letter I received from the superior of the Capuchin monastery at Restigouche, in which he directed attention to the condition of the roads in that reserve. It lies on the banks of the Restigouche river, opposite the town of Campbellton, and is surrounded by a splendid network of highways built by the province of Quebec. Ste. Anne de Restigouche is a pilgrimage centre to which thousands of people come from all parts of Quebec and the maritime provinces to visit the church, which is one of the oldest in the district. According to this reverend gentleman the roads within the reserve are in very bad shape, though the surrounding roads are in good condition. He complains that nothing has been done for some time and in the letter which I sent the minister he makes a number of suggestions which I think are very timely. These Indians are the survivors of the Micmacs of the old days, who reside on the Restigouche. They earn their living by doing a little cultivating and by acting as guides for fishermen on the salmon rivers in my county and the surrounding districts. Some of them work in the sawmills when they are in operation, but there is not very much of that work at present. This gentleman points out that the reserves are in a pretty neglected condition, not through any fault of the agent but because of lack of funds, and I should like to know what the minister intends doing this year.

Did I understand my
lion, friend to say there were two reserves?

Yes, Restigouche and
Maria. They are both in Bonaventure county.
There is the sum of $125 in the estimates for the maintenance of roads in the Restigouche reserve.

Is there anything for the
Maria reserve?

No.

Supply-Indian Affairs

Does the minister imagine he will go very far with S125 on a reserve about ten miles square? I think the amount is much too small, and I hope the inspector who goes down there periodically will look into the matter and see if the amount cannot be increased. Apart from the Indians themselves thousands of people visit that reserve to see the shrine of Ste. Anne de Restigouche, which dates back to the middle of the eighteenth century, and it is not to the credit of the Indian department to have the roads and sidewalks in the condition in which they are at present. I hope the minister will see his way clear to improve matters. Then, I should like to ask this question: Is the same system being followed whereby teachers are paid to educate the Indians in these two reserves, or have changes been made lately?

Practically the same
system is in existence to-day as has been operating for some time, namely day schools are provided on the reserves, and the teachers are paid from parliamentary appropriations.
I should like to know if the hon. member referred to roads on the reserves which might be considered provincial highways, and used by white people and Indians, or whether he had reference more particularly to roads maintained in the interest of the Indians themselves. I make this distinction because the committee will readily understand that in the Indian reserves there are different types of roads. Since a policy of provincial highways has been inaugurated throughout the length and breadth of Canada many such highways pass through Indian reserves. When speaking of roads we must keep those provincial highways in mind as contrasted with the roads built in the reserves purelj' for the use of the Indians themselves.

The Perron boulevard which encircles the whole Gaspe peninsula passes through the township of Mann in which this reserve is situated. That road is in first class condition, and this year, owing to the celebration, Gaspe will be visited by thousands of people from all parts of the continent. The roads to which I have referred, however are those local roads which run through the reserves, following the Restigouche river. From the letter which I received I would judge they are in very bad condition. Of course, any person going to church in that section of the country must pass along the roads on the reserves.

While I have no desire to criticize the manner in which the department has carried on its administration, may I say to the minister that the tendency to educate the Indians in an attempt to bring them to our standard of living seems to me rather far fetched. Three centuries of the history of Canada have proved it is useless to try to make white people from Indians. Of course, I am not criticizing the minister in this connection, because I understand the educational system is carried on in close cooperation with the different religious denominations. I think however that after three centuries of experience we must come to the conclusion that it is useless to try to bring these people to our standards of living, and I doubt very -much whether in those efforts we are improving the conditions under which the Indians live. Instead of doing that I think we should try to develop their natural tendencies and dispositions. For instance, the Indian people are highly artistic and have given to Canada an example of artistic work which cannot be surpassed. While I admit that some kind of education is needed I should like to see some change introduced whereby the system of education among the Indians would follow more closely their needs, requirements and disposition. For instance, why should we not help them to foster the development of those handicrafts in which they are past masters. I do not think those Indians who have been educated to our standard of civilization are very happy.
In passing may I say that there seems to be a tendency for the city people to educate the farmers according to city standards. Certainly -I do not wish to create any ill feeling between city and country people, but I believe that different standards of teaching and of education should be set for the different modes of living. I should like the minister to give some thought and consideration to these views. Perhaps with his long experience and with his influence he might try to experiment along the lines I have suggested.

In a word, the hon. gentleman is questioning the administration of the education system of the department, and I have no quarrel with his observations. As he and other hon. members are aware the system of education among the Indians is not the result of a day's growth. Rather, the system now in vogue has developed through a great -many years. My reading has taught me that the educational system started through the efforts of the different church denominations to Christianize the Indians. In their zeal those people sent missionaries who, I believe, found themselves handicapped in
Supply-Indian Affairs

their work. In order to help themselves they established schools, feeling that if they could gain the support of children when they were young, thereby getting them under their control, they would be in a position to Christianize those children and bring them to the white man's mode of living. Various churches put that system into effect. At a later point, finding the financial burden of education rather heavy, they applied to the dominion government for assistance. That assistance was given and throughout the years has been increasingly given.
The system education in effect to-day might be divided, broadly, into two classes, namely the residential and the day school systems. The churches prefer the residential school system. In those schools the child is taken in at a comparatively tender age, about six or seven years, and remains there until he or she has reached the age of sixteen or seventeen. During that time they are instructed in practically the same subjects as are the pupils in the white schools. The day school system is run very much on the same plan as the public school system of our provinces, and it is in existence on those reserves where such a plan can be put into effect. The committee will realize that on many reserves it is impracticable to have a day school system. The Indians in some cases occupy a large area of land and it would be impossible to get the children to school. On the other hand, the population of a residential school may be drawn, as it sometimes is from the whole provincial area. The hon. member has expressed the opinion that the system now in vogue is wrong in certain respects and that these people should be taught their native handicrafts. That is a debatable question. For instance, the handicrafts system is best known by the Indians themselves, and those best qualified to teach these handicrafts are the parents of these Indian children. In many reserves these handicrafts have been preserved and are to-day one of the main sources of income of the Indians. I need only mention the St. Regis Indians, who are proficient in basket weaving, and Indians on other reserves who are proficient in making snow-shoes, Indian moccasins and so forth. I may say to the hon. member that I have given considerable thought to the question whether these handicrafts should be taught in our residential schools at the present time.
Fostered, not taught. I agree with the minister.

My hon. friend says that
he agrees that these handicrafts should be fostered rather than taught. I was merely going to point out that if these handicrafts were to be taught in the schools it would impose upon us a financial burden which we are not able to bear at the present time because we have all we can do to maintain the present system. But as a matter of fact we are encouraging handicrafts among these people, and I agree with my hon. friend that we should in certain cases foster these handicrafts. We must, however, be careful not to generalize because while certain Indians are proficient in basket-weaving or the making of snowshoes, not all Indians are. They have their different abilities the same as the white people, and because one Indian is a basket-weaver it does not follow that every Indian is a basket-weaver. But in order to encourage this work we are making grants of a total of $7,500 this year for prizes at exhibitions for Indian handicrafts and agricultural produce.

Do those grants cover all
the reserves or apply only to a certain area?

The grants are made to
certain fairs and institutions.

I presume on this item we

I would recall to the minister that last year the minister brought in a bill that was very much debated and very much amended, and finally passed, with reference to the compulsory enfranchisement of Indians. I think this would be an opportune time, if a report has not already been made in some form that I have missed, for the minister to report what has been done under the authority of that act.

It is not near

We should know what was
done under that bill. While I am on my feet I wish to refer to a newspaper report in regard to a matter on which the minister probably has some information. It was reported that certain Indian youths of eighteen or nineteen at a place called Shubenacadie were subjected to treatment that, judged by the standards of British justice, would seem to be monstrous. It was alleged that certain youths were soundly thrashed in order to extort confessions of the theft of a small sum of money. I would like to know if the minister has had any report on the matter and can inform the committee what action

has been taken, because if the facts were as reported I have no hesitation in saying that those responsible should receive the utmost penalty the law provides. In dealing with the Indians we must not insist in treating them altogether according to our own standards. They must be treated with a good deal of consideration for the fact that their standards are not as high as we claim ours to be, and we should set them an example of humanity and justice rather than an example of extreme cruelty such as would seem to have been practised on these boys.

Answering the first question of the hon. member for Lisgar, in the fiscal year 1933-34 there were 44 enfranchisements of Indians under section 114, I think it is, of the act, but none were enfranchised under the section of the act that was amended last year.

For the information of the hon. member and the committee I may say that a commission is being appointed under the Inquiries Act to make the fullest inquiry into and report upon all the circumstances surrounding the alleged flogging, and upon that report the action of the department and of the government will be based.

I was very glad to hear
the minister say what he has said with regard to no compulsory enfranchisements having taken place under the act passed last year.

Not under that amended
section.

But there have been 44

Under section 114, I think it is.

I hope that from time to
time as the estimates of the department comfe before the house those of us who are fortunate enough to be here will receive a similarly satisfactory report from the minister that no compulsory enfranchisements have taken place under the amendment which caused so much discussion in this house last year. At that time I expressed myself, as did some others, as being very strongly opposed to that class of legislation, particularly as applying to these people. I am glad that the minister and the department have not found it necessary to resort to what I looked upon as a very harsh, very drastic and very unnecessary piece of legislation.
I see that the estimates here include relief, agricultural activities, roads, bridges, dyking, education and so forth. I would like some information in regard to these matters, and perhaps it would make the discussion a little less disconnected if I indicated the information I should like to receive:	First of all,
as to the amount expended on relief last year for the Indians throughout the dominion, and how that compares with the amount spent on relief in the previous two years; also the manner in which that relief was expended. I happen to come from a section of the country in which a number of Indian reserves are located containing I think as good a type of Indian as can be found on this continent. I hope the minister's experience during the stress of the last few years has been that the Indians have not required more in the way of relief than has been required by white people in many municipalities. The amount expended in the Restigouche reserve was S150.

That is estimated for the present fiscal year.

Could the minister give me the expenditures for the present fiscal year for the Muncey, Oneida and the Chippawa reserves? Could he also give us the amounts expended in previous years? The reserves to which I have referred contain many miles of roads and like most Indian reserves, they lie alongside rivers. Consequently the construction of highways and bridges is perhaps a little more difficult than on more level ground. Much industry has been expended by the Indians themselves in keeping up their own roads on the reserves and in some cases they have worked without pay. I think better results could be obtained from the money expended on relief by increasing the amounts for highway construction. A number of bridges are at present in such a condition as to be almost dangerous to the travelling public and I should like to know if there is to be a program of reconstruction of bridges on the reserves to which I have referred.
