I am sorry I have not the items for relief toy themselves but I may say that we have been able to keep our relief within reasonable bounds. Since I have had the honour of administering this department it has been my constant endeavour to inculcate in the minds of the Indians through the administration of the various officers that they should make every effort to make themselves self-supporting rather than to lean upon the state. I think we have been fairly successful in -that connection. The hon. member desired to know the amounts in the estimates for certain reserves in Ontario. I find that the estimates for tihe Caradoc agency contain the sum of S500 for the improvement of main roads in the Muncey reserve, $250 for the improvement of main roads in the Oneida reserve and $250 for repairs to culverts over Turkey creek in the Oneida reserve. I might explain that in addition to parliamentary appropriations for the construction and maintenance of roads and bridges, this work is also carried on with expenditures from the band funds. For instance, on the Six Nations reserve we expect to make a considerable expenditure for the maintenance and improvement of the roads in that reserve and the money for this work will be obtained from the band funds, supplemented by a donation of forty per cent from the Ontario government.
I understand $7,500 is being granted for gratuities by way of agricultural prizes.
Prizes for agricultural and handicraft exhibits.
Would that include ploughing matches and that sort of thing?
Yes.
Does the department carry on competitions open to Indians only?

Prizes are given for Indian work and these prizes would go to Indians only. Both systems are carried on in connection with the ploughing matches. There are some matches in which Indians only compete while in others they compete with whites.

I think some of the best ploughing done in my part of the country is that done by Indians from the reserves to which I have referred. These Indians have been successful in taking a number of prizes in open competition with the white men in the community. In my opinion one of the best ways of encouraging proficiency in agriculture is to provide for a certain amount of money to be expended on prizes along the line of ploughing matches and that sort of thing where the competition is limited to those who are on the reserve.

I am informed of an item which may be of interest to the committee: at Yanderhoof in British Columbia the Indians carried off practically all the first prizes in open ploughing competitions, so I can readily understand the interest of the hon. member for West Middlesex in this matter. The Indian, if he sets his mind to it, can do in many lines of endeavour just as efficient work as can his white brother. I am well aware of that from my knowledge of Indians who inhabit a reserve in my constituency. I know in white settlements adjacent .to that reserve, if the white people can employ Indian labour at harvest and haying times, they prefer them to any other class of labour they can get. That is of course a matter which gives us in the Indian department great encouragement, because we feel that these people are capable of being very proficient in different lines of endeavour.

I should like to have some information from the minister regarding the Lennox Island reserve. As he is probably aware it is on a small island and a ferryboat has to be maintained there with a wharf on each side. I think the wharf on the mainland side is kept up by the federal Department of Public Works. I am not sure whether the minister's own department maintains the wharf on the island where the reserve is. I should like to know in what condition are the wharves, the ferry and the road?
We have in the estimates for this year the sum of $175 for repairs to roads, bridges, etcetera, generally for the reserves in Prince Edward Island.
Could the minister give to the committee the amount expended for relief on the Six Nations reserve during the past three years?

I am sorry I have not that information at hand but I would be glad to get it and give it to the hon. member.

Supply-Indian Affairs

There are one or two matters I would like to put before the minister with regard to the Indians around lake Winnipeg. These fellows have a habit of wandering in to see me occasionally, I do not know why. There was a complaint made to me some time ago by the Indians on the Fisher River reserve that leases were given by the government, probably the provincial government, to fish on the Fisher river. Those fishermen occupied all the ground in the mouth of the river and after taking out their nets full of fish including a great many small ones, the latter were discarded and thrown dead back into the river or discarded generally. The Indians said that the fish discarded by these fishermen would feed the Indian tribe who were themselves more or less without food. I do not know how much truth there is in that, but I thought it worth while putting before the minister. The Indians complain that these fishermen discard enough fish to feed the tribe over the winter and it is deprived of the possibility of fishing for itself. That is the first item.
The other one is this-and I have mentioned a portion of it to the minister privately-in the lowlying land around the delta of lake Winnipeg, the mouth of the Red river as it empties into the lake, there is a very wide stretch of hay land, and between the town of Selkirk and the mouth of the river there are many settlers of foreign extraction, Ukrainians. They are petty farmers; all of them have herds of milch cows and raise a little bit of grain. Those hay lands are leased as far as possible according to the requirements of the farmers in that district, but the complaint is made that a number of men from the same establishment will put in applications for licences and instead of the hay being liberally divided among the various farmers of the district, it has all got into the hands of a very few. I do not for a moment suppose that the minister would have any knowledge of these matters, but there is without doubt an abuse of administration and they are worth while looking into. For that reason I put them before the minister just for what they are worth.

Tire hon. member has brought up a question which has not previously been directed to my attention, namely, the matter of fishing in lake Winnipeg at the mouth of the Fisher river. There is, I know, an Indian fishing station at that point utilized by the members of the Fisher River band and those who live on the Peguis reserve. Whether since the transfer of the natural resources to
the provinces, the regulations in regard to fishing come under the jurisdiction of the provincial or the dominion government, I am not in a position to state, but I am rather of opinion that the regulations in regard to this fishing rest with the provincial rather than with the dominion government although I speak subject to correction on that point.

If I may interrupt the minister on that point: if by any chance through an abuse of the regulations the' Indians are being deprived of their winter food which very largely consists of frozen fish, I think the matter ought to be looked into by his department.

I was about to remark when the hon. gentleman interrupted me- and I do not object to the interruption-that I would be pleased to inquire fully into the matter and find out under which jurisdiction it rests; if it rests with the province I shall be glad to bring it and the remarks made by the hon. member to-day to their attention and endeavour to secure a satisfactory solution of the difficulty. I know the Indians depend to a great extent in many cases on fishing for food particularly in the winter time, and I know what this means to the Indians of that particular reserve.
In regard to the licensing or the granting of permission to cut hay on what is known as the old St. Peter's reserve, as the hon. member has stated, he did take the matter up with me privately some time ago, and I issued to the department instructions which I think will solve the difficulty, if there has been any. Those licences can be granted earlier in the season than has been the practice hitherto, or at least I know of no reason why they should not be. Apparently the hon. member thinks, if that is done, the difficulty will be overcome.

Another point that I wish to draw to the minister's attention is that a number of applications will come from one establishment, so that the hay on the old St. Peter's reserve instead of being fairly well distributed amongst the Ukrainian settlers of that district practically all falls into the hands of two or three.

Those who have first
claim upon this hay are, I believe, the Indians who own lands in the vicinity. After that permits are given to the various white settlers. I am informed that the division has been fairly equal among the white people. However, I shall be glad to make inquiry
Supply-Indian Affairs

and get a list of those who have received permits. The intention is that those hay lands would be used fairly amongst the white settlers in that district after the Indians have obtained their allotment.

In item 176 there is
provision for a grant of 8100,000 approved by parliament in the session of 1926-27. Will the minister explain what that is and for what it is used?

This money is included
in the estimates yearly, following an arrangement arrived at after the parliamentary committee had inquired into the matter in the session of 1926-27. I was not a member of the house at that time but I think I am correct in saying that this sum of money is paid to the Indians of British Columbia in lieu of treaty money. That is, certain Indians in other parts of Canada receive certain annuities, amounting to 8234,000, which sum is provided by statute. In order to put the Indians of British Columbia on a fair footing with other Indians in Canada this special amount is provided by parliament from year to year. It is used for hospitalization, education and medical services.

What consideration has
been given, if any, to the building of roads or bridges in any of the Indian reserves in the constituency of North Battleford? There are quite a number of Indian reservations in that constituency, some very large, and I would like to know if anything is to be done in the way of giving the Indians on them better transportation facilities.
There is no amount provided in the estimates this year for roads or bridges on any of the reserves in Saskatchewan.

I think the minister
is acquainted with the fact that on many of the reserves in Saskatchewan, and I presume all reserves in western Canada, the fur catch is becoming less and less, and the money returns from this activity becoming smaller year by year. If the Indian is not making satisfactory progress in the cultivation of land and the rearing of cattle and such ways of making money, his standard of living must be going down. Can the minister throw any light on the results of education of the Indians on these reserves in that respect?

As the hon. member knows, the Indians in certain parts of Canada were granted certain rights in regard to hunting, fishing and trapping. In the western provinces prior to the transfer of the natural resources

the dominion of course had complete control. When the natural resources were transferred to the western provinces a clause was inserted in the agreements providing that the Indians were to have the right to trap and hunt on unoccupied crown lands. The provinces, I believe, or some of them, claim that they have the right to grant leases to or licence individuals to run trap lines on these crown lands, and that having so leased or granted licences over these lands they are no longer unoccupied crown lands. That is a position with which we do not agree. But, as the hon. member will realize, it is a matter of considerable importance to the Indians. I am glad to tell the committee that the fur catch generally this last season has been very satisfactory, in fact better than for some years, and as the prices of fur were also higher, the Indians, or those at least who follow that mode of making a living, are in a better position than they have been for the preceding three or four years.

I thank the minister for that answer. Even if the Indian is forbidden to go on crown lands to catch furbearing animals I believe that under the educational facilities on some reserves at any rate he is being trained and developed to be more capable of making his own living successfully.' It may be that no matter what amount of education you give an Indian he still remains an Indian, but the idea is to develop the possibilities of manhood in him and make him able to adjust himself to his surroundings and thereby make him a better citizen and less dependent on the state. I think the education of our Indians on the reserves has that for its object-, and I believe that as long as that object is kept in view we shall have at least fair success in educating the Indians.
But to proceed may I say that the Meadow Lake Indian reserve is located on the Meadow river over one hundred miles north of North Battleford. I think any one who knows that reserve will admit that the land there is as good land as there is outdoors in Canada. I understand that a few Indians occupy that reserve-. On it now there is the town of Meadow Lake, with a population of about 1,500. The Canadian Pacific Railway has built from a point on the Prince Albert-Shellbrook line of the Canadian National into Meadow Lake. The Canadian Pacific now has connection from Prince Albert, and I might say North Battleford, into Meadow Lake. There was a move to see whether that Indian reserve can be bought from the

Supply-Indian Affairs
Indians in order that there may be settlement on it, and not simply a few families as at the present time. The idea would be to pay a fair price to the Indians, distribute the money among them and have them relocate farther north or in any other direction, on suitable land. Some representations must have been made to the minister with regard to this matter, which has been hanging fire for years, and I think there should be a report in the department. I should like to ask the minister whether any action has been taken or if any action is contemplated with regard to this very important matter.

Would the hon.
gentleman tell us roughly how many settlers might be expected to avail themselves of that opportunity?

I could not say exactly
but I should think there would be a considerable number of settlers. There are only a few Indians located on that land, and my idea was that the Indians could be fairly dealt with by having that land purchased and the money distributed among them. It would be a great help to the progressive Meadow Lake settlement, which has taken on new life in the last few years, since the railway went in and settlers from the south have gone north.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Approximately how large is the reserve?

I do not know exactly
but I should think the minister could give us that information.

I have not the exact
figures before me, but the reserve is of considerable size, comprising several thousand acres. I may say that this matter was brought to my attention, on the last occasion about two years ago, I think, when representations similar to those made by my hon. friend were submitted to me by correspondence. The position is very simple, in one sense of the word. The Indians own these lands; they belong not to the white people but to the Indians, and the department is unable either to lease or sell any Indian lands in the Dominion of Canada until a surrender is obtained from the Indians themselves stating the terms and conditions upon which the land may be leased or sold.
Might I ask the minister if the whole proposal could be halted by one Indian who refused to sign?

I have not the Indian
Act before me and I cannot quote the section, but I think I am correct in stating that the surrender is based upon the majority vote; that is, if a majority of the male members of the band over twenty-one 3'ears of age vote in favour of a surrender such surrender is made. Then, of course, the department is in a position to make whatever deal may be considered most advantageous under the circumstances. I may say that the Indians on this particular reserve to date have not been willing to surrender their lands, and in consequence nothing can be done in regard to the matter.

I understand the position of the minister and the department. I was under the impression, however, and the minister can correct me if I am wrong, that some few years ago practically every Indian was willing to sign, with I think only one exception. I do not know whether the matter actually came to a vote.

Of course I speak subject to correction, but to the best of my knowledge no vote was ever taken. There are certain very definite rules and regulations in regard to how the vote shall be taken, and to the best of my knowledge no vote was taken. Individuals may have expressed themselves as being favourable to the surrender of the lands for lease or sale, but when it came to the question of voting they might vote differently. I think we have all had a little experience along that line during our canvasses; certain individuals have told us they were for us, but when we saw the results at that poll later we found that they did not come up to our expectations. Perhaps the same thing might happen in this case.
I would point out further that in the course of his remarks the hon. member suggested that these Indians might be moved further north. There is no land further north in the province which is within the gift of the dominion government. Since the transfer of the natural resources all such land is under the control of the provincial government and we have nothing to do with it.	.
Of course the government could buy land further north or in any other direction if they saw fit to do so.

The minister is correct in stating that the majority prevails, and that brings to mind a grievance which has been brought to my attention from time to time and which I should like to discuss on behalf of the Indians. I am dealing with British Columbia only, because I am familiar with conditions in that province.
277S
Supply-Indian Affairs

The department recognizes the Indians as their responsibility and takes care of them in the matter of relief. The Indian knows that no matter what happens, even though he may have nothing at all, if he becomes destitute or ill the department will take care of him. Here is the situation that arises at times, however. A railway wants to buy a piece of land from the Indians for a right of way, or perhaps the land is needed for a factory site or a sawmill site. In any case a body of white men want to buy a piece of the Indian reserve, and under the law the consent of the Indians must be obtained in the way indicated by the minister. I think of recent years, though it was not so when I was first an Indian agent, the rule has been that if the land is sold for a given sum half that sum can be distributed in cash to the band while the other half is put into a fund allotted to that particular band and no other, it being argued quite properly that they have alienated a piece of their communal holdings. So they get half the cash and the other half goes into a fund. That is explained to the Indian, and he is told also that there will be interest accruing on that amount. Too often the idea is held out to him that if he wants to use that money to put up a community hall or do fencing or something like that he may get the interest on the money or sometimes the capital itself. This is what happens very often, however; perhaps interest accumulates for a year or two and then a cash payment is made to the head of each family. Two or three years later they apply for another payment, but they are told there is no more interest money. They ask what has become of it, if the Indian agent has stolen it, because that is usually their first reaction. The agent tells them that he has taken that interest and used it to pay for the relief bills of the band.
From the point of view of the department there is some plausibility to that argument; they say this is the Indian fund and the interest should be used for the jrelief of the band. The Indian says-and this is very logical-the next time you go to him and ask him to consent to the alienation of a piece of his land, "What shall it profit me; why should I oblige the white man? I only received the small cash payment and did not get the rest of the money." The Indian decides that the department will take half the money and use the interest to pay the ordinary relief bills of the band, which the department would pay in any case, and the Indian has enough intelligence and understanding to see that point. The band on the next reserve,

who do not sell their land, are cared for in exactly the same way as the band who alienate part of their land, but in the one case the department pays for the relief while in the other case the relief comes out of the funds of the Indians themselves. As a result the next time we want the Indians to part with their land they are extremely unwilling to do so, and very often it is very important from a public point of view that Indian land should be acquired.
I do think faith should be kept with the Indians. If the department say the money is to go into a fund for the band, that fund should be kept subject only to the control of the band. You would not think of selling a piece of the reserve in order to pay the storekeeper's relief bills, but this fund takes the place of the piece of land that has been sold, and it should be regarded not as a fund for relief but as a part of the reserves of the Indians. Any interest accruing on it should go to the Indians at the absolute discretion of the band. That has been a sore point with the Indians ever since I have had anything to do with them, which covers a period of more than thirty years, and as the encroachment-I do not mean that in an improper sense-of the white man upon their lands becomes greater it becomes more and more necessary to alienate parts of these reserves. You have that increasing trouble because the Indian thinks he is not getting a square deal. You have taken his money from him, and you do not give it back. I think the minister understands the point.

Yes, I believe I have a fair knowledge of the matter about which the hon. member has spoken, and I may say there have been certain difficulties in connection with it. When the land or Indian property is surrendered for sale an amount-I think it is up to one-half-may be used for distribution pro rata among the members of the band. Sometimes half the amount will be given, and at other times the Indians themselves will, in the surrender, specify the amount to be distributed.
Not exceeding one-half.

Yes, not exceeding one-half. We will say that they do not think it would be in their interests to take one-half, when they surrender on the condition that a certain amount shall be distributed among different members of the band. The hon. member has said that the amount of money left is placed in a certain fund to the credit of that particular band. In that statement he is correct. The money is placed to the

Supply-Indian Affairs
credit of the band, and on it the dominion government allows five per cent interest. The fund thereby accumulates, if the increment is not used for relief, for the building of council halls or for other Indian purposes. Sometimes, not very often, a distribution from that fund is made. The hon. member has said that that is not a fair treatment and that the funds and the interest should not be used for purposes of relief. That is an open question, and one in connection with which different opinions might be held. I would point out that the Indians in one reserve, namely the Blackfoot in southern Alberta, are practically self supporting, that is to say, no demands are made on the department for relief. Through their own efforts they are able to provide a living for themselves, and in addition they pay their own hospitalization services. The only money spent on that reserve from parliamentary appropriations is for the upkeep of the schools. The funds of the band are used for all other purposes.
That is an exception.

As the hon. member has said, it is an exception. To some extent however it is true with other reserves and other bands in Canada where band funds are held. These interest funds are used for the benefit of the Indians. I have stated to the committee and to the house on many occasions my belief is that the Indian should be in a position to stand on his own feet and through his own efforts provide for himself. That is the policy which has guided me in the administration of the Indian Department. I do not believe that it is good either for the Indian or for the white man to have the feeling that whether he works or not, or whether he has funds or not, he may throw himself upon the state and that in any event the state is bound to look after him. I realize that a responsibility rests upon the Indian department to look after the Indians and, when they are unable to do it for themselves, to provide them with the necessities of life. At the same time I reiterate that not only should he be encouraged but he should be directed and led along the lines of self reliance. I am not certain whether the hon. member has argued that these funds should not be used for the purposes of building a council hall or for relief purposes. In some instances the bands hold funds running up to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The Blackfoot Indians of southern Alberta have a fund amounting to considerably more than a million dollars. It could hardly be argued that a band with such 74726-176
valuable assets should be kept on relief from parliamentary appropriations.

Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of my remarks I said I was referring to the province of British Columbia where band funds run to only a few hundreds, or at the outside perhaps a couple of thousand dollars. The minister has said that he believes the Indians should be taught to stand on their own feet. No one can possibly gainsay that statement; it is a truism. I suppose his statement applies to standing on their own feet financially and socially; I think it should also apply to standing on their own feet morally. And how can you teach them to do that when you break faith with them? There is no question at all that the bargain is made with these Indians that they shall have half the money in cash, if they wish it, and that the other half will be put into a fund under their control. You break faith in doing anything else. The minister has asked what I want, and he has asked whether or not I want relief to be paid out of their interest money. I do not care what they do with their interest money, provided the consent of the band is obtained. The money in the fund is the property of the Indians, just as the land was their property, and you should no more take away that money-because the land is represented by money-than you should take away the land.
The treaty made with the Indians has from time immemorial recognized that we must provide the Indian with relief when he needs it. We know that. We have two bands placed side by side, one of which has not sold any of its land or its reserve, and they get relief when they require it. We cannot get away from that fact; that is in the treaty. But the band a few miles away have been induced by the arguments of the Indian agent to part with their heritage, their land, and a substitution is made of so much cash in the bank. Then the department comes along and although they could not alienate the land without the consent of the band they alienate the interest money and use it to pay bills which otherwise they would have had to pay, anyway. Is that fair? Certainly, spend it on a community hall or for relief, if you like, but only if you can get the vote of the band to that procedure. But I say the money belongs to them, just as the land did. The money represents a piece of their land. Then the department comes along- they would not dare do it if a white man was concerned because in that event they would be taken before the courts-and they say, "We will take this money, which is yours,

Supply-Indian Affairs

and we will alienate it, and pay our relief bills with it." That is not fair or reasonable. In years to come when, in a hurry, you want a release from an Indian band you will have trouble in getting it. That is the point. Get the consent of the Indians to alienate their money, if you can-I know you cannot-but do not take it from them simply, I was going to say, by force of arms, actually by departmental regulations.

Is there any difference in principle between the use of the interest on the money to the credit of the Indians and the use of the natural resources which the Indian has not alienated? I am going to ask the minister whether it is not a fact that timber on the lands of some of the unceded bands in northern Ontario is being used now by the Indians to provide themselves with relief. The timber standing on the land is the property of the Indian, and as I understand it it is being used by the Indians-and I am speaking subject to correction-and sold for the purpose of providing means for relief or living through these difficult periods. Am I right or wrong; I should like to be clear on the point?

The hon. member is quite correct. In some instances Indians are surrendering their timber for sale, and from the proceeds they gain a livelihood. In other cases the Indians themselves cut their own timber and utilize the proceeds from the sales for their living.

I think it is to be hoped that the department will not for some time, lightly undertake the release of any further Indian lands in this country. I have lived in western Canada for over fifty years, and if my information is correct the Indian has always got very decidedly the worst of the deal. Some considerable number of years ago the surrender of the St. Peters Indian reserve was obtained from the Indians for a certain consideration in cash-I do not know the exact terms of the contract-but the Indians were relieved of a fairly good piece of agricultural land and were moved away from lake Winnipeg to a place among the rocks and muskeg where there is no timber and very little land of value, and there to-day they are starving. They are the most scrofulous, the most tubercular people I have even seen in my life. They have very little means of making a living except by fishing in the summer, and when the water freezes in the winter they have a very blue look-out for a living. That St. Peters reserve got into the hands of a few speculators. The Indians 
were moved off and the speculators failed to make anything of the land, and a great deal of it is lying idle to this day. Since then the Indians have been seeking to come back to this land but they have never been permitted to do so, although there are very few settlers on it. So it is with some reason that I say it is to he hoped that the Department of the Interior will hesitate before they seek the release of any more Indian lands.
Not the Department of the Interior, the Department of Indian Affairs.
Well, the Department of Indian Affairs.

Following the remarks of my hon. friend from St. Boniface, so far as the selling of any portion of the Meadow 'Lake Indian reserve is concerned, if through force of circumstances, the encroachment of population or the development of the district, something must be done, then I would say that the department should be the major factor in any change that is made with respect to this land. Surely the Indian department should be able to guarantee an absolutely fair deal for the Indians. If it could not, what department of the government could?
May I say that in any suggestion I have mads with regard to moving Indians north, south, west or east, my underlying thought' was always that the Indians would be paid every cent that was coming to them for their land, that the Indian Act would be abided by and a vote of the band taken, and that in every case, if anything were done, the Indians should be dealt with fairly and in their own interests. Might I ask the minister, if it is the case that a vote must be taken before any part of a reserve is given over for any other purpose than that of an Indian reserve, how did it happen that the Canadian Pacific Railway got control or purchased thirty or forty acres of the Meadow Lake Indian reserve and built a station upon that land and constructed a right of way through it, together with yard facilities upon a certain amount of it? Did they buy that land from the Indian department? Were the Indians satisfied to sell it, or does a deal of that kind come under what we might term, in railway language, the right of eminent domain?

My answer to the hon. gentleman some time ago in regard to the surrender of the lands in, the Meadow Lake reserve, that the department was not in a position to deal with -these lands until they had been surrendered by the Indians them-

Supply-Immigration
selves, I should have qualified by saying that under certain conditions, when it is in the public interest, expropriation proceedings may be taken. Whether the Indians surrendered their land that it might, be sold to the Canadian Pacific Railway, I do not know; but I rather think that those lands were expropriated, as can legally be done under the Railway Act.

I understand that the Indians of the Squamish reserve, North Vancouver, during the fiscal year 1932-33 were allowed several thousand dollars from their fund, for agricultural development. Would the minister explain how that was handled and if it has been a success?

The money has not all been expended as yet. We are carrying on certain agricultural experiments on that reserve, and we are moving slowly in the matter. I have read certain reports from the agent and the inspector that appreciable progress is being made on that reserve in agricultural pursuits.
Answering the hon. member for St. Boniface, I am in general agreement with the remarks which he made in regard to the alienation or sale of Indian reserves. We have in Canada now an Indian population of approximately 115.000, and in some of the provinces the Indians are being so cribbed, cabined and confined in very small areas that it is difficult indeed for them to make a living. I wish to assure the hon. member that before the department considers the sale of any -Indian reserve or any portion thereof in the Dominion of Canada the question will be most minutely inquired into, as we are fully seized of the importance of retaining these reserves for the use of the Indians.

As the charge has been directly made that the Indians have never been paid for the St. Peters reserve, that they have been paid only a minute fraction of the consideration involved in the undertaking-I have never inquired into the details-I think now is a good time for the minister to make a statement on the matter.

I- have not the figures before me but I can say that the report which the hon. member has received is untrue. I shall be very glad to get, and to give to the hon. member, a full statement of the financial 'consideration and of the financial adjustments that have been made since the sale of that reserve.

I would like to say a word to the minister on a subject I raised 74726-176 }
last year when the Indian estimates were up. What progress, if any, is being made in the negotiations which I understand have been entered into by the Indian department, with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec particularly, in relation to setting apart that portion of Ontario and Quebec north of the height of land for the use of the Indians in the taking of fur-bearing animals and game birds for profit? These Indians are the natives of that area and they should have the exclusive use of the country, otherwise they will soon become wards of the government in the sense that they will have to be maintained all the time by the government. The quantity of furs which can be taken out of that area by the native Indians, who were there before we were, would enable them to make a living and preserve the game life of the country at the same time. If that part of the country is going to continue to be overrun by the class of white trapper now trapping that country, the game life will be soon extinguished and the Indians forced to depend upon the state entirely. There are no other means by which they can make a living.
They could have farm lands.
There are no farm lands north of the height of land.
What amount is being set aside for roads in the Stony Point and Kettle reserves?
There is an amount of $695 for improvement of roads, 8300 for repairs to bridges and culverts and $300 for maintenance of drainage systems in the Kettle and Stony Point reserves, Lambton county.

What is meant by inland supervision? You have boundary inspection, and inland and seaport supervision.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
We have agencies at
Winnipeg, Hamilton, Toronto, Calgary and various other inland cities where agents of the immigration department are resident.

But we were told a few moments ago that the services of the department are divided into three sections, east, west and Pacific coast, and we were given the figures in each case. In the east it cost $466,604 for permanent employees, $32,274 for temporary employees and $13,325 for part time employees. In the west the figures were $129,000, $20,268 and $4,401, while on the Pacific coast they were S80,610, $7,569 and $6,548. We pay large salaries to the employees in the various divisions mentioned by the minister, and I am surprised to learn that in addition the department has to provide such huge sums as $33,000 for the inland agencies, $28,000 for the seaport agencies and $73,000 for the work on the boundary, as well as the other items mentioned. I submit that the minister should give us more details as to how these contingencies are arrived at, and whether they could not be curtailed. We are told that the government has practically stopped immigration, that we do not want people from foreign lands to come to Canada, but there is a reduction of only $177,712 in this item; we are still called upon to vote the huge sum of $1,239,288. If we have stopped immigration, as the government say we have, why do we have to spend this large sum of the people's money? I should like the minister to answer that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The decrease in the vote as compared with last year is $183,712. From the immigration figures of a few years ago it will be seen that in the last five years the total vote has been decreased by probably fifty per cent. It is quite true that immigration such as was invited and encouraged in the years prior to 1930-31 has diminished very materially. Whether or not it has been the part of wisdom to invoke those restrictions to the extent deemed necessary by the government is, of course, a matter of argument; everyone is entitled to his own opinion. But bear in mind that in the immigration department files containing the history of every landed migrant are kept for the purposes of determining his right to stay during his probationary period.

How far do these files
go back into history?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
They have been kept
since the department was set up. I think that would be shortly after confederation, at which time it was a branch of the agriculture department. Following that it was a branch of the interior department and finally was set up by itself as the immigration department.
Supply-Immigration

These files cover the migrants who have legally landed, and they are very necessary to-day, as hon. members of the chamber well know, because I doubt if there is a member who has not at some time or other seen me with respect to relatives of or those closely associated with people legally landed in Canada with a view either to returning them to the land of their nativity or allowing their near relatives to come to Canada-
I have not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
There are some exceptions; the hon. member for Quebec East says he has not done so, but I think he is almost alone in that regard. It is necessary that we have these facts, because in Canada we have a very complex population and these files are of great assistance in determining whether or not and to what extent their relatives or friends in the old land or in other countries can be admitted. So it is very necessary that these files be preserved for use when investigations are made to determine whether or not the government or the department would be justified in following a course looking to the uniting of families or the admission of friends, and matters of that kind.
It may seem that since there is practically no immigration there is no work, but I would leave it to the judgment of the ex-Minister of Immigration, the hon. member for West Edmonton, whether or not the department does not provide ample opportunity for the activity of the minister and the officials who are taking care of this situation as best they can. The figures will disclose a great shrinkage in expenditure over the last few years, and each month there is a further decrease where decreases can be brought about and where departmental officials can be adjusted so that their activities will be put to good Service. When vacancies occur it will be noted from the report that has been tabled that they are not filled except in very special cases.
Does the vote include medical inspection of immigrants?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I assume the hon. member has in mind the medical inspection overseas of intended migrants.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: And at ocean ports. That does not come under this vote, but is dealt with by the Department of National Health.
It is not under the Department of Immigration at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No.

There are two small matters
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister; the first being in regard to the employment of immigration officers during the busy season. At the moment I am not going into the question of salaries, but I must say a complaint has been made to me that in the last two years the services of seasonal men have been cut down, and that men who are employed the whole year through are getting

S upply-Immigra tion
considerable overtime, thereby cutting out seasonal employment. Looking through the records I find that in some instances the overtime runs as high as S450 or $500. In my view that is a considerable amount of money to be received for overtime, especially in these days when so many men are out of employment. I think consideration should be given to those men who are engaged during the busy season, and that if possible they should be given an opportunity to assist during the busy seasons at the ports of entry.
While I am on my feet I should like to voice another complaint which has been made, namely that the Canadian Pacific Railway have been bringing engineers from the old country to fill positions on their steamships on the Pacific coast. Last year they brought in six engineers from the old country and placed them on the ships on the Pacific. The complaint is made that in these times of unemployment no men should be brought from the old country; it is not fair to allow men to be brought in to fill these positions, when plenty of competent engineers are idle on the Pacific coast. I have affidavits under my hand from at least six competent engineers who were formerly employed on Canadian National ships, and who for the last one and a half or two years have been idle. They feel aggrieved, and rightly so, that a company like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should bring men from ships travelling between Great Britain and Atlantic ports and place them on the Pacific coast, at a time when employment is so scarce here.
I know that what is done in the United States can have little bearing on this country, but one superintendent who two years ago was in charge of the Canadian National docks in Vancouver who was ordered to go to the United States and take charge of Canadian National property in Seattle where we have property valued at at least $1,000,000. After being in that city for two weeks he was ordered out of the country because he had no permit and was told not to come back. I believe some explanation should be given as to why engineers were allowed into the country when there are plenty of engineers on the Pacific coast competent to fill the positions.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member has been given a good deal of consideration. The point arises as to whether or not persons working in international waters should be accorded privileges, if we may call them such, and whether or not the engineers on the coastal steamers are qualified to carry
on under the laws which have relation to the operation of those steamers. I recall that at one time representations were made to the department with respect to some engineers on the Pacific coast. The information I was able to gather with respect to this group-whether it is the group the hon. member has in mind I am not prepared to say-was to the effect that they were unable to qualify for service on the steamers upon which they sought employment. If my recollection serves me correctly, opportunity was given to these men to take out the necessary certificates in order to qualify and some difficulty arose in connection with adopting that course. However the matter is still under consideration and investigation in the hope that any real grievance may be removed.
With respect to part time employees may I say I believe it will be found that across Canada there are very few employees receiving overtime pay. Unquestionably in some cases an employee will work a day or two longer than his usual hours of employment, and receive some remuneration for such overtime. But generally speaking, and in so far as humanly possible, overtime has been eliminated. I shall consider, however, the representations made by the hon. member in order that as many temporary employees may receive work as is consistent with efficiency.
Mr. MeINTOSH: I am pleased to see the minister back in the house again, and may I express the hope that with renewed health and energy he may continue his work to the end of the term. I have a question or two I should like to ask. It is generally admitted that immigration into western Canada has been curtailed seriously during the last four years. Having that fact in mind may I ask the minister how many ports of entry there are from the United States into the three western provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
There are about thirty ports.
Mr. MeINTOSH: Does the minister mean that there are that many ports along the international boundary stretching from Ontario to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
In the western division, yes.
Mr. MeINTOSH: How does that number compare with the number in 1930, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No material change.
Mr. MeINTOSH: There would be an inspector at each of these ports of entry, I presume, and just what other staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It sometimes happens that the immigration and customs services can be combined at different ports, each department bearing a portion of the charge. Perhaps the following information will be sufficient for the hon. gentleman, although I can give the names of the officers as well if desired. We have in Manitoba an inspector at Banner-man; one at Winnipeg, with a considerable staff; a part time inspector at Cartwright, Crystal City, Goodlands, Haskett, Lena, Coulter, Piney, Snowflake, Windygates. Then in Saskatchewan we have a part time inspector at Northgate, Big Beaver, Big Muddy, Carievale and Climax. A number of others, such as North Portal, Coutts and Emerson, make up the total for the western ports that I have mentioned.
Are these part time inspectors customs officers as well as immigration inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I think in nearly every case those mentioned are customs officers as well.
Do they get two salaries or only one?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: They have a very difficult time getting one salary.

They have these two services to perform, and as I understand the minister's statement the customs work is the heavier. These staffs are required because of the dual duties they are performing. Do I understand that to be the real reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

Wherever by reason of the amount of work to be done and by reason of the customs work and immigration work dovetailing into each other it is possible to unite the two services in one official, we have tried to do that across Canada for the obvious reason of saving expenses.

Are there any agencies still maintained in the United States and other parts of the world looking after immigration to Canada? If so, where are they located, who is in charge of the different offices, and what are the salaries paid

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In 1930 the government of the day had about fifteen agencies in the United States spread from coast to coast, and a number of agencies on the continent of Europe and in the British Isles. It was thought desirable to close the agencies in the United States, and they have all been closed. It was also thought desirable to close the offices on the continent of Europe, and they have all been closed with the exception of the offices maintained' for the purpose of civil and medical inspection of those who have a legal right to enter Canada. We have three offices on the continent, at Paris, Antwerp and Hamburg. Certain curtailments have taken place with respect to the offices in1 the British Isles. We have offices at London, Liverpool, Glasgow, Bristol, Inverness, York and at Belfast, but the staffs in all these offices have been very materially reduced. It was not thought desirable that these offices should be closed because certain valuable contacts were made in the United Kingdom during the course of immigration activities. We get so many very highly desirable people from the British Isles that it was thought desirable to maintain these offices, although they are being maintained with greatly reduced staffs. There is also an office at Hong Kong through which are passed all people from the orient who have a right to come to Canada.
Could the minister tell us who is in charge of the offices at Paris, Antwerp and Hamburg?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Mr. Belanger at Paris, Mr. Mitchell at Antwerp and Mr. Chapdelaine at Hamburg.
Are there any other officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There may be a stenographer, but I do not know.

Has the minister any idea how much these offices cost at Hamburg, Antwerp, Paris, the British Isles and in the orient? The minister mentioned salaries paid in Canada as well as contingencies, but I do not think he gave particulars of the salaries or expenditures in connection with the offices outside of Canada.

I should like to have that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I shall get it for my hon. friend.

I think the department is quite right in maintaining a certain number of immigration agencies throughout the British Empire. We can maintain empire contacts through these agencies. The minister stated that nothing is being done in the way of immigration activities in the United States. I should like to know how many immigrants came into western Canada from the United States during the last year or so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It would be difficult for me or anyone to state exactly how many immigrants came into western Canada from the United States. It is within the realm of possibility that an immigrant might come into western Canada from the United States and then, not liking that part of the country, move to eastern Canada, or vice versa.
I hardly think that would happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Perhaps we will have to agree to disagree. On page 10 of the report of the Department of Immigration and Colonization which has been tabled are figures which will furnish an answer to the hon. gentleman's question. Unless the committee desires it, I should like to be relieved from reading the figures on to Hansard.
I thought that would be rather an easy question to answer. If we are doing no work to get people into western Canada from the United States I should like to know just how many did come in.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: During the year 1933, 13,196 people came into Canada from the United States. I think we can congratulate ourselves that the movement of desirable immigrants from the United States is very substantial.
That was the idea back of my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
We have a splendid
country.

In January of this year the following resolution was passed by the British House of Commons:
That this house is of opinion that the time has now come when His Majesty's government should get in touch with the governments of
the dominions with a view to putting forward a scheme for the voluntary redistribution of the white peoples of the empire and the stimulation of shipping and trade under the flag.
Could the minister state whether the British government has got in touch with the Canadian government in connection with that resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The answer is in the negative.
Do I understand that this government has not been approached by the government in England with a view to promoting that scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No.
It is all on paper.

When the estimates were up before the minister gave the number of people who had been sent back to the British Isles. I asked a question at that time, out of which another question arose. I wanted to know the number who had requested to be sent back to their country of origin. The minister was able to give me the figures for the British Isles and he said he would look up the figures for the other countries in Europe. Has the minister any information to give the committee at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The answer to that question would involve a great deal of detail. It is all given in the report of the Department of Immigration and Colonization for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1933. Table number 54 on page 65 gives the countries to which people were returned and the reasons for their being returned.
In the amount mentioned for contingencies is included $9,000 for Chinese; what is that spent for?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The Department of Immigration and Colonization is charged with the administration of the Chinese Immigration Act. For reasons which I am sure are well known to hon. members, this act is very difficult of administration. The item to which reference has been made has to do with the administration of that act.
Is that act administered by this government in conjunction with the United States or China, or is it under the control of this country alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
That act is a statute of the parliament of Canada. It was passed before I became a member of the house and I think before my hon. friend was a member.

I do not think so, because I would remember.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It was designed to control Chinese immigration into Canada. I shall not take up the time of the committee in going over its various sections as they are there for any hon. member to read.

That statute was passed several years ago and I do not know just what are its terms. I should like to know in what way that $9,000 is to be spent in connection with the administration of the act. Is it to be spent to keep Chinamen out of the country, or to send them back, or to prevent them from committing misdemeanors, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Sometimes it is to send
Chinese back to their country; sometimes it has to do with legal proceedings in connection with their right to be in Canada; and there are of course travelling expenses in connection with these investigations and other small incidental matters such as stationery, ink, postage stamps and so forth.

That is true, but in view of the minister's statement there are some other figures that need further explanation. He says that that amount is spent for stationery and also for sending Chinamen home. In the contingencies he has another item of $135,000 for deportations. Does he mean to say that besides the $135,000 under the heading of contingencies in connection with deportations, there is still some of that amount of $9,000 that goes to deport Chinamen? He speaks about stamps and stationery. There is under contingencies another item of $6,000 for the head office at Ottawa. I suppose the expenses in that connection are for stationery and such matters. Some further explanation should be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Regarding the item of
$135,000 for deportations, there may be an overlapping so far as the administration of the Chinese Immigration Act and deportations generally are concerned, but if so, it is to a very slight degree; the item of $135,000 is deportations generally without, in the main, including those under that act.

If the minister cannot
give more detailed information I have to take what he givers me, but I must tell the committee that I am not very well satisfied with the explanation given. I hope next year, when these estimates come up, we shall receive more detailed information.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I hope to be here at that time.

There may be a change and then we shall have more information.
Regarding the item of $3,700 mentioned under contingencies, for immigration of British children, how is that sum accounted for? Have we a scheme for bringing young British immigrants here?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
That item is the result
of an agreement entered into between the British government and the government of Canada that preceded this one, with respect to bringing British children here, under which certain obligations were assumed by the Canadian government with respect to the aftercare of those children. If the estimates for past years are examined, they will be found to be rapidly decreasing. The British children who come in under the agreement have, generally speaking, done very well.

How long will these
agreements be operative?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The agreements, so far as bringing in the children is concerned, have expired, but the obligation to take care of them, that is the after-care, has not expired. This vote, however, indicates by its reduced size that the work is pretty well finished. I hope it will not be long before we can not only take care of those in Canada but see many more of the British boys come here.

I understand that this
sum of $3,700 is for looking after British immigrant children in Canada. How many of those young boys came here this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: None.
Last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: None.

There are some other
items to which I would like to draw the attention of the minister. I said a moment ago that under the heading of contingencies the sum of $6,000 was mentioned. This is a big amount when we have also all the salaries of the officials; I am not complaining about their efficiency, but I should like to know what this item of $6,000 is for. The minister told us that under the item of $9,000 for deporting Chinese, stamps, stationery and other matters are included. Six thousand dollars is a very large amount and I would like to have some definite information as to how it was spent.

speechtext:
This item would cover
such matters as travelling expenses of executive officers of the department. There are some expenses of the head office at Ottawa

that will be charged to this vote, the details of which I cannot supply because I do not have them at hand.

These people must be
travelling a great deal. Under the heading of contingencies, as I have stated before, we had 873,000 for the people who look after the boundary immigration service, $33,000 for the inland service, and $28,000 for the seaboard service. Besides all these we have S4,000 or $5,000 or $6,000 for travelling expenses from the head office to the various parts of the country. The minister ought to be in a position to give us detailed information as to how this amount of $6,000 is arrived at. If the department has any motor cars at the head office, how many would there be? Who are the officials or special inspectors or other officers, if there are any, who travel, and if they were on special cases, what was the purpose of their travels here and there throughout the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I confess I cannot give
the details of the travelling expenses of the major officials of the department. Certainly the chief commissioner has been to each coast on a number of occasions; the deputy minister has made certain trips, as has also the assistant deputy. In fact, I think if the auditor general's report were examined, it would be found that I have made certain trips and probably, although I do not know at the moment, they were charged to the department; I have not the figures under my hand. But this, I take it, is an appropriation that is common to every department of government where one cannot go into the details; in every department an item of this kind is voted and has been since there were departments. It is a responsibility of the minister and those acting with him to see that a vote of this kind is properly spent and used for contingencies for the expenses of the major officials of the department during the course of their work. Surely the hon. member would not ask me to try to forecast for the next twelve months what a vote of this kind is likely to comprehend. I frankly confess I cannot do it.
What are the conditions and regulations in regard to the entry of any immigrant into Canada? In other words what are the admissible classes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Perhaps I may answer in this way; there has been no amendment of the statute itself, and no amendment of the regulations with respect to intended migrants from the British Isles and from the United
States. There have been amendments relating to the continent of Europe, limiting those who will be admitted to (1) the wives and children of migrants legally landed in Canada who upon investigation have been found willling and able to receive their relatives, and (2) migrants who desire to come to Canada, who upon investigation have been found to be provided with sufficient money to carry on agricultural activity in Canada, who have had an agricultural background in the land of their nativity and who in the opinion of our investigating officers are desirable people to be admitted. That is as briefly as I can state the act and regulations as they obtain at the present time.

What about the case of the children of immigrants who have been allowed to enter this country? I feel personally that there should be some latitude in regard to allowing say a son or daughter of an immigrant now in Canada to come into the country. Certainly such a one is to be preferred to an immigrant who ostensibly comes to farm but soon drifts into the city to engage in some calling there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Cases such as the hon. member has outlined arise very frequently. Perhaps a son or a daughter not eligible under the present regulations desires to enter Canada, and the parents here desire the migrant to join them. When representations are made to the department concerning such cases an investigation is conducted, and if it is found that the family is a desirable one-of course I have to rely on the information I can get from the safest sources that I can resort to-and the case falls outside the regulations, a recommendation is made to council in order to procure the admission of the person in question.
Has any bond to be given by the parents in a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No bond is required unless it is a case, such as arises sometimes but not frequently, where the child is physically or perhaps mentally defective. Then a bond would be required in order to assure ourselves against the possibility of that child becoming a permanent public charge.

I may say to the committee that I have had the privilege of making representations to the minister on one or two occasions with regard to cases of this kind. The minister received these representations in a splendid way, and if I remember correctly the children were admitted, of course to join their parents and engage in agricultural work in the dominion.
