Can the minister tell the committee how large is the sum, generally speaking, which is looked upon as requisite for that purpose, or if there is any set figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is a very difficult question to answer; it must lie very much in the discretion of the officers who carry on the investigation. I am sure hon. members will readily realize that if they were at one of the ocean ports or on the continent looking over a possible immigrant, using their best discretion they might well turn down a man with $50,000 and let in a man with 50 cents. Perhaps the man with $50,000 would lose it in a very short time and become a charge on the community while the other chap would start to make his small capital grow. We have to use discretion, and we do not lay down any arbitrary rule. It is most difficult to determine just what should apply in each individual case.

Then there is no minimum sum required? I based my question on the minister's statement that one of the conditions, and perhaps the main condition, was that the immigrant should have that sum which, in the opinion of the department, was requisite in order to give him some prospect of success, and I wondered if any minimum was set. I understand that there is no minimum?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I can perhaps answer that by saying that no agriculturist has been admitted with less than $1,000 in cash after he arrives here, and in almost every case it is a great deal more.

This is a very large vote, amounting to practically $1,250,000, and according to the minister very few immigrants are being admitted, while the restrictions covering their admittance are very rigid. I have been wondering if it would be possible for this department to branch out on another line that might be considered an innovation. Before mentioning that, however, I should like to direct to the attention of the minister the matter of the British boys who have been brought to Canada. I believe he said they were quite satisfactory. I remember that a few years ago we were told that these boys were given some training in Great Britain prior to being brought out here. I believe they were put in schools or on farms under agricultural instructors and given at least the first principles of agricultural activities before being sent to this country, and I think perhaps they were put on farms out here for instruction as well. At any rate, in general I think the scheme was quite satisfactory.
For the past two or three years the minister also has been pursuing what he calls a land policy, which I endorse. While some

Supply-Immigration
take exception to it I do think that any person with an agricultural background placed on the land with not too heavy an indebtedness over him has at least a fair chance of making a living. The matter I was going to bring to the attention of the minister is this: there are a number of young boys in our own country who have not an agricultural background. Some of them are university graduates; some have graduated from our collegiate institutes. I have had young boys ask me how they can get a start so as to make their way in the agricultural industry. Some of them would not know which end of a horse to put forward or where to put the collar on a horse, perhaps, but the point I had in mind was this: would it be possible, out of this large sum of money, perhaps in conjunction with our experimental farm system, to establish training schools for such boys who have not an agricultural background, giving them a year or two of agricultural training and then starting them out on our farms as the British boys were started, in the hope of placing a number of them where they would have a chance to make good? I wonder if this thought has ever been brought to the attention of the minister and what he would think of such a scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The suggestion made by
the hon. member is one that might very well be given serious thought by everyone interested in this country. In this rapidly changing world we have found that perhaps industry does not offer the same job security that we had hitherto expected. Previously activities along the line suggested by my hon. friend have been confined largely to private organizations within and without Canada. The activities of the department, with regard to trying an experiment, let us call it, along the line suggested, commenced in the fall of 1930, and the hope was that facilities could be provided to bring to the attention of Canadians just where lay their surest hope of security as far as the home unit was concerned. We saw our cities with many jobless persons, a large percentage of whom had come from the rural sections of Canada, as every hon. member knows. A casual review of the movement from the rural districts to urban centres during the past forty years disclosed a rather arresting picture, and unquestionably in this country there is a very large disequilibrium of population, particularly having regard to the advance and mechanization of industry. The suggestions made by the hon. member might very well merit the attention of every hon. member in the chamber, because, in my opinion, in very large
measure his suggestion offers an outlet and security not only for the youth who is growing up, but for even middle aged persons who find themselves without any means of livelihood. In 1930 the department outlined what has now been termed the back to the land movement, but which at that time I called colonization at home. The purpose behind the movement was to try to induce those who were able, to take advantage of what Canada had to offer. It was an encouragement to people who had funds of their own, and who saw those funds gradually dwindling in rents paid in the cities. I believe that in that effort we met with measurable success. Then, as hon. members will recall, in the following year aid was given to those who understood what it was to make a living on the land -not a fortune, but a living-so that they might be taken off the unemployment shelves.
The suggestion made by the hon. member goes somewhat further. I can readily appreciate its implications, and I have a considerable appreciation of the benefits which would flow from a long range policy of the type which he has suggested. I have given careful consideration to it. As to whether or not this is the time to begin there may be differences of opinion. In my view one thing is sure, namely, that no sounder or saner policy could be advocated or invoked by any government in 'Canada than to equip young men who have a flair for farming with knowledge which will enable them to 'take advantage of such opportunities as our country affords. All of us cannot go into mining; we all cannot go into the professions. Our country is just as good as we make it-perhaps it is just a little too good for most of us, because there are too many who will not take advantage of the opportunities it affords, but would rather take the very comfortable attitude that the world owes them a living. I think the day is rapidly coming when people will have to turn to the advantages the country offers, go at it and work. A long range policy along the lines suggested by the hon. member cannot be developed in a moment. It would be most desirable to equip our young men who care to take up that vocation with a scientific background, if you like, or at least with a mechanical background, so that they may know how to do their work, and so that if they desire they may take advantage of the Opportunity afforded by the farm lands in Canada.

I did not intend to take part in the discussion to-night, because I have a great deal of sympathy for
Supply-Immigration

the position in which the minister finds himself, due to the fact that in previous governments I occupied that position on various occasions. But I do wish to say, Mr. Chairman,, that when I hear professional men and some farmers talking about the advantage of training young men to go on the land I get a little bit fed up-yes, just a little bit fed up, because for some sixty odd years I happened to be a farmer. We farmers find it difficult to keep our boys, trained to farming, on the land. Why? Because they cannot make a living on the hand'-.that is the difficulty. When I hear hon. members who have spent their lives in farming express approval of a scheme for training young men who have been prepared for other vocations in life, to do farm work, at a time when tens of thousands of boys are leaving the farms to go into the legal and medical professions, I am somewhat annoyed. Let me say to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that until farming is put upon a different basis you had better quit advocating the sending of men to the farms.	4
Change your policy.

Such talk makes me tired. Only the other day I entertained a young man who had been brought out from England under a scheme of immigration. A bright young chap, he discovered very soon after arriving in Canada that in comparison, with law, farming was a poor vocation. He is now training for taw. This young man was in Ottawa only a few days ago with a group of young people from the university of Alberta who were taking part in. the drama festival. I asked him why he did not stick to farming, in view of the fact that he had come to Canada with the avowed purpose of doing so. He said, "Mr. Stewart, it did not take me long to discover that farming was not a profitable vocation in Canada. I decided to enter the university of Alberta, and, backed by the financial assistance of my people, take a legal training."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: He has my sympathy.

I can say this to the minister, who is also a member of the legal profession that when he gives advice to young men to choose agriculture, as it exists in Canada to-day, in preference to any other profession, he is not giving them very good advice. I make that statement despite the fact that we have a good many medical and other professional men on relief to-day. In my opinion agriculture has

never had a fair deal; certainly it has never had a fair deal in all the years I have been engaged in it. Remuneration from agricultural activity in Canada, despite what professional gentlemen may say, is not and never has been at all comparable to that received from any professional vocation. When I hear hon. members advocate that young men should give up professions of various kinds and, backed by the government or by some other authority, go into agriculture, I say to myself "Well, for heaven's sake, if they knew what they were talking about they wouldn't advocate any such thing." As Minister of Immigration and Minister of the Interior I have sat on the government benches and have been bombarded by hon. gentlemen who then sat on this side of the house with requests to bring people to Canada to engage in farming. Because of the necessity of the occasion I was forced to spend money for that purpose, knowing in my heart that when I did so I was possibly lending my assistance to a scheme which was not required in Canada. Because of modern inventions and modern machinery we have enough agriculturists in Canada to-day to produce far more than we can consume, yet we are asked to spend money to take young men from the cities and the professions and place them in a vocation which in Canada is already overcrowded. Why have we 200,000,000 bushels of wheat which we cannot sell? I submit that if we could sell all the live stock owned by farmers today, over night they could increase their production to the point where we could not possibly dispose of it. I get a bit tired of hearing gentlemen advocate schemes under which they w-ould put people on the land to earn a livelihood. Perhaps some people in the cities to-day who have been trained in agriculture could go on the land, on a small holding, and make a living, but that is all they will make. I know western Canada and I know eastern Canada. The statement used to be made that we westerners produced great quantities of wheat and then went to California to spend our profits, but in the most prosperous days not three per cent of the western farmers found themselves in a position to go to California. I know something about Ontario, the banner province of Canada, and I know that under present conditions very few farmers in this province are far removed from the sheriff, who may step in any day and sell them out. Let us face the facts squarely. We are all in difficulties. I do not say that the professional man is having an easy time, but when

Supply-Immigration
you tell me that the professional man, who may have a smattering of agriculture, can be trained to take his place and succeed amongst men who have followed agriculture all their lives, you are telling me something that is not true. My hon. friend may indeed know a great deal about agriculture. He has been trained in the profession of the law, but let him go out on the farm-I will give him one in Ontario, and I guarantee that in five years he will have starved to death. We might just as well be honest and plain about this thing. Ask any practical farmer in this house, no matter how much he has had in the way of financial support, and he will tell you that in a period of twenty-five years, unless he has been mighty careful, his remuneration at the end of that period will not in any way 'be comparable with that of the professional man-I am not speaking of the top-notcher, but the ordinary, everyday doctor or lawyer. And the reason we cannot keep our boys on the farm is that they know these things, and they want to enter one of the professions. I have three boys; only one of them is on the farm, and I have the greatest difficulty in keeping him there, because despite the fact that his brothers are in receipt of only meagre incomes he still thinks they are much better off than he is. Yet the government is asked, and when I was in the government I was asked, to train young men who have no knowledge of farming in order that they may go into agriculture and the professions may not be overcrowded. I repeat that I get just a little bit tired of that sort of thing, Mr. Chairman. I do not care what branch of agriculture you go into, the fact remains that agriculture has had to bear the burden and heat of the day ever since I knew anything about conditions in this country, and just now this government, apparently sensing the real situation, are presenting a marketing bill in order that they may help our distressed producers of natural products. Why are they doing it? Because they realize full well, just as the minister does, that the agriculturist to-day is in a very serious situation. The government are beginning to realize today more than they ever did before that unless they do something for the farmer his chance of earning a livelihood on the farm is very precarious indeed.
What is the remedy? What are you going to do about it? Put more of them on the farm? I have never believed in all the years I have been in this house that we could pay our debts and ease the burden of taxation that is upon our shoulders by further immigration, because every new citizen means a
new burden. I think I am warranted in making that statement. The poor duffer who comes to this country or our own citizens who have been born and raised in urban localities have a mighty slim chance of succeeding on the farm. Better train these young men in mining or lumbering or something else, but for heaven's sake do not spend money to send them into agriculture under conditions as they exist to-day.

I have no right, of course,
Mr. Chairman, to speak on a question pertaining to farming, but the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichaeil) brought forward, as I think the minister admitted, a very good suggestion that was worthy of consideration. I did not hear anybody suggest that professional men should be taken from the cities and put on the farm. The suggestion was that young men of Canada, not men learned in the law or in some other profession, should have the means to go on the farm. I have never attempted to discuss farming except in 1926 when I did venture to express the opinion that if the farmers of the west would quit wheat mining and become real farmers they would not have hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat on their hands. I told them they would if they continued wheat mining, and they have got it now. I am not speaking as a lawyer, for I am not a lawyer. I was not brought up in the legal profession, which may or may not be good for me. I am only speaking as a five cent business man. But I do say to my hon. friend from West Edmonton that the trouble with the farmers of the west is that they were not farmers but wheat miners. The men in the west to-day who are real farmers are not in any great difficulty. If the information is of any value to my hon. friend, I may say that my father was a dry goods man. He had three sons and brought them up to the dry goods business, which we nicknamed the rag business. We have stuck to the dry goods business, and I think the great mistake in this country is that the man and the woman on the farm with three sons, instead of encouraging them to stay on the farm, have the idea that one must be a lawyer, another a doctor and the other a minister of the gospel. That is the key to a lot of the trouble. Keep them on the farm, and the affairs of this country will be in a better state. Do like my dear old dad did-bring your sons up to your own business.

I just want to correct my hon. friend in one thing. When he talks about wheat mining he is talking
Supply-Immigration

absolute rot. He is talking about something he knows nothing about. He knows no more about it than I do about the dry goods business, and that as nothing. It is all right for the easterner who has made his pile and can spend it in, California to talk glibly about the wheat miners of the west. But that is a pure myth. There is just as much mixed farming in western Canada to-day as in eastern Canada. But fortunately in the west we happen to have a country in which we can produce considerable quantities of wheat. We find ourselves with a considerable surplus, or rather the government finds itself with it, unfortunately. But when my hon. friend makes a statement like that about wheat mining it is pure unadulterated rot.
Mo-. SPOTTON: Order.
I say that advisedly, Mr. Chairman. It is pure unadulterated rot.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I submit that it is unparliamentary for a member to say that another member is talking rot. I ask for your ruling.

I notice, Mr. Chairman, that you hesitate to express your opinion on the point of order. I would hate to offend my hon. friend, but his statement calls for strong language, and so far as I am concerned I propose to express my views in the strongest possible terms. I have no apologies to make. When I hear hon. gentlemen rising and talking in this house about matters which, as I have pointed out, they know nothing about, know no more about than I do about the dry goods business, then I am constrained to use strong language.
I never assumed to know anything about farming.

May I say this to my hon. friend, and perhaps he will think this a strong statement. I was raised in Ontario before I left for the west. I operated a farm which my father had operated before me. My only background is farming; I have no other business except that I happen to be a member of parliament. The situation of the farmer in western Ontario may have been maligned and in some respects misrepresented, but with few exceptions the position of the farmer in the old province of Ontario is just the same as that of the farmer in the west.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend says, "oh, no," but I have made some

very close and careful inquiries and I say that advisedly.
You are wrong.

No, I am not wrong. To put a man on a small piece of land with the handicap of even $600 is placing too much upon his back. The minister has followed me in the administration of the Soldier Settlement Act. Who were the soldier settlers? They were young trained farmers who had joined up, served their country and came back. The moment I took charge of that matter I claimed that no boy, no matter what his training or no matter how well he was equipped, could carry such a burden of indebtedness upon his shoulders. He has not been able to do it and that is the reason why there have been so many failures. It is an utter impossibility. What is going to happen with this back to the land movement? As long as conditions continue to be serious and difficult in the urban centres these people will stay on the land and eke out a living, but the moment the wage scales mount in urban localities, there will be a desertion from the farms to the cities.
Speaking for myself alone, I do not believe in encouraging people to go on the land, either through state aid or in any other way. If they want to go on the land of their own volition and know something about it, let them do it, but you will never make a success of putting people on the land under state aid. There has never been a more deplorable thing than the attempt to settle trained farmers on the land under the soldier settlement scheme. These men were not novices; they knew their business, yet they could not make it go. Under present conditions no farmer in Canada is going to make a success unless some relief is given, and I know whereof I speak. This applies not only to western Canada but to eastern Canada as well. Yet hon. members stand up and say that farming is a lucrative occupation, that a man can make at least a living out of it. You can if you are mighty careful, but I would hate to say the rest of it. I do not believe in any back to the land movement aided by the state, but I do believe in a back to the land movement by people who know something about fanning, who know the difficulties they will have to face and the privations they will have to endure. At no time during the sixty years that I have lived has the farmer received a square deal. I say that advisedly. It is amusing to hear hon. gentlemen in the professions, in the trades and in industry telling people how to live upon the land. I

Civil Service-Salary Deduction
have listened to such talk in the legislature and in this House of Commons until I have become tired of it.
There is no doubt we are passing through serious times but that is because fifty per cent of the people who are on the land are not able to make a livelihood. Until these conditions change neither the farmers nor the rest of the population will be in a very happy position. Unless something in a real way is done to assist our farmers and agriculture, the difficult times through which we are passing to-day will continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A point of order has been raised by the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) as to whether an hon. member is in order in saying that another hon. member's utterances are unadulterated rot.
Will it help my hon. friend if I cheerfully withdraw that remark?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I cheerfully do so, because I have made my statement.

More than ten years ago I remember saying in this house, when we were debating this very question of immigration, that the greatest danger facing the western farmer was that of overproduction. I did not get very much support-no more than a horse laugh from some hon. members. We have gone too far in the spending of money to bring in immigrants to produce more wheat and cattle. I have a certain amount of sympathy for the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and I congratulate him on the case he has made out to-night. Eleven years he was being badgered in the house to spend more money to bring in more farmers. We were told we must bring in farmers only, we must keep out the professions, the dry goods merchants and all such; they did not need any competition, but we did need more farmers to produce more agricultural products. When we asked who would eat all this stuff we were told there was an unlimited market. We have now found out that that is not so. To suggest that we ought to train more men and encourage them to go on the land seems to me to be

well, I do not know any parliamentary language in which to express myself. It is absolute nonsense to talk about such a thing. We know what happened with the soldier settlement scheme, and yet it is proposed that we enter upon a scheme whereby a lot of men will be put through the same kind of misery. A few weeks ago I gave the house the average income in 1932 of all farms in Canada; according to the bureau of statistics it was only $600, and out of that amount had to come interest, taxes, insurance premiums, machinery repairs and all that. There is an average of six and one-half persons per farm, and these had to live out of the balance. To suggest that we should encourage people to engage in agriculture under conditions like that is pure nonsense, and I am sorry I cannot use language strong enough to express what I really think about it. This fall good beef cows were selling in my constituency at one cent per pound. Any hon. member ought to know that any man engaged in producing fat cows to sell at one cent a pound is going into bankruptcy more quickly than he could go any other way; he would probably be better off if he went and gambled on the stock market or bought a sweepstakes ticket. If the government want to do something to better conditions in Canada, let them regulate the packers and take them off the farmer's back. Let them see that the farmer gets a decent price for his products. To think of spending our good money-perhaps it will be raised by the sugar tax-to put people back on the land to produce more wheat or cattle or other agricultural products, I say again is nothing but pure nonsense. I am surprised at the minister encouraging such a move, let alone proposing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARY DEDUCTION ACT-RESTORATION OF TEN PER CENT CUT TO EMPLOYEES RECEIVING $1,000 OR LESS
speechtext:
When we were in committee on the last occasion, the hon. member for Rimouski raised a point with respect to a provision in clause 3 and the point was also raised by the hon. member for Gloucester. The provision will be found in line ten on page 2 of the bill, as follows:
And there may be paid out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund such sums as are not otherwise provided for and are necessary to provide the full amount of compensation of those to whom this proviso applies.

Civil Service-Salary Deduction

The objection of the hon. member for Rimouski and also of the hon. member for Gloucester was that this gave unlimited powers of appropriation from the consolidated revenue fund and there ought to be a specific vote for the purpose. On that occasion I pointed out that a similar provision was contained in a number of bills. I instanced at the time, without having any record before me, that a similar provision was found in the Old Age Pension Act. But may I point out also that the same provision is found to-day in the following acts or statutory provisions:
Government Employees' Compensation Act.
Subsidy payments on Canadian coal.
Dominion Fuel Act.
Election expenses.
Gratuities in lieu of leave on retirement- National Revenue employees.
Cost of loan flotations.
Railway grade crossing fund.
Furthermore, may I point out that in the Salary Deduction Act of 1932 the same provision appeared, as will be found in subsection 2 of section 5 of that act which provides:
The superannuation of any contributor whose compensation does not exceed $1,200 per annum shall be paid out of any unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
Identically the same provision will be found in the Salary Deduction Act which we passed last year. Therefore it will be observed that there is nothing new in the principle of this provision. I do not, however, wish to say that' because this has been done in previous acts and in previous years by governments of varying political complexions, therefore of necessity we must continue the practice, although I must say that there is a very sound reason for it. It is impossible in the nature of things to make an exact computation, and this is to provide an elastic sum to meet contingencies which cannot with accuracy be appraised in advance. The danger if you provide a fixed sum is that you may have too much or too little. If you have too little you do not provide sufficient to accomplish the purpose you have in mind, and if you provide too much you have an invitation to utilize a larger share of the appropriation than may be necessary. I do not wish to stand upon the order of procedure so far as the suggestion of the hon. member for Rimouski is concerned, and if he feels there is any more protection to the public treasury I am quite content that a limitation should be proposed. With that object in view, if the committee desires to put a limitation on the amount, I have had an amendment prepared accordingly.

There is only one other point with respect to the wording of this subsection-and perhaps it is worthy' of note-it is that the provision for payment of the amount in the terms in which it is provided in the bill limits it to the second proviso whereas the appropriation should be available for both provisos. Perhaps this feature ought to be provided for by amendment, but with respect to the limitation of expenditure I am quite prepared to abide by the wish of the committee.

I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is in his place, but I regret that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) are not in their places. I remember sitting on the other side a few years ago-it may seem like a hundred years to some but in fact it is only three or four years ago-when the present Minister of Justice, the present Minister of Railways and the present Prime Minister sat on this side of the chamber. At that time they claimed with tears in their eyes that a civil servant should have at least $100 per month in order to bring up a family under Canadian standards. If that statement was right then, it is right to-night. In view of that statement I wonder if the Minister of Finance would not make the amount $1,200 instead of $1,000. Of course, he was not in the house at that time and was not responsible for the sins-I should not call them sin3, because I agreed with them
or the gospel of his colleagues. I know the Minister of Jinance will say that increasing this to $1,200 will mean quite an additional amount. The same thing was said in connection with the old age pensions. After that legislation was well on its way through the house hon. members of the Conservative party who were opposed to old age pensions advocated that the pension should be not $20 a month but $30. They also wanted the age limit lowered from seventy years to sixty-five years, and some wanted it brought down to sixty years. That would have cost about $1/9,000,000, but these suggestions were made in an effort to kill old age pensions. I know the Minister of Finance can advance the legitimate argument that increasing this limit to $1,200 will cost the federal treasury several millions of dollars, but the fact remains that some years ago $1,200 was the minimum set upon which a civil servant could live, and the same holds true to-day.
Progress reported.
